source: Miller (1956) The magical number seven, plus or minus two
finding: Miller separated two limits. Absolute judgment of one stimulus dimension is limited by information (bits). Immediate memory is limited by the number of items. The title number seven was a rough pattern across both, and Miller himself doubted it.
numbers: Absolute judgment (bits): pitch 2.5, loudness 2.3, salt taste 1.9, position in an interval 3.2-3.9, curvature 1.6; mean 2.6 bits (SD 0.6), about 3 to 15 categories. Digit span about 7 items (about 3.3 bits each, about 23 bits).
quote: Absolute judgment is limited by the amount of information. Immediate memory is limited by the number of items.
limits: Read via a WebFetch summary of the psychclassics full text, not the raw page. Miller called seven a possible 'pernicious, Pythagorean coincidence'. Cowan (2001) later argued the item limit is nearer 4.
agent_relevance: Do not quote 'seven plus or minus two' as a hard limit for the agent. The useful idea is that limits are in chunks and that recoding into chunks changes capacity.

source: Miller (1956) The magical number seven, plus or minus two
finding: Span depends on item type, so a fixed bit budget does not explain memory span. Recoding into larger chunks raised span a lot.
numbers: Binary digit span about 9; monosyllabic words about 5 (a constant-information rule would predict 2-3 words); words are worth about 10 bits each. Smith's recoding: baseline about 8 decimal, 9 binary, 7 octal; after drilling Smith recalled 12 octal digits, about 24 binary digits (2:1 recode), about 36 (3:1), about 40 (4:1 and 5:1).
limits: Smith's gains came from drilled subjects (the author himself among them). Untrained recoding gave less than the octal span predicted.
agent_relevance: Chunking is the lever: a scaffold that recodes many raw items into a few named units (a compact state summary) lets a fixed-size workspace hold more.

source: Hitch, Allen and Baddeley (2024) The multicomponent model of working memory fifty years on (QJEP 78:222-239)
finding: The 1974 starting question: do the resources behind short-term memory span serve as a general working memory in thinking? Method: simulate a span-deficit patient in healthy adults by loading short-term memory with irrelevant items, then test reasoning, prose comprehension and free-recall learning.
numbers: Result pattern the same for all three tasks: moderate but far from catastrophic interference when the memory load was at span, little or no interference when the load was well below span.
quote: moderate but far from catastrophic interference when STM capacity was filled to capacity
limits: Retrospective by the model's authors, not the 1974 chapter itself. The 6.2 MB scan of the 1974 chapter had no text layer and was not read.
agent_relevance: A full store does not stop reasoning, so storage is not the whole bottleneck. Something shared (control) is. For our agent, context length is not the thinking limit.

source: Hitch, Allen and Baddeley (2024) The multicomponent model of working memory fifty years on (QJEP 78:222-239)
finding: Baddeley and Hitch posed a limited-capacity central executive, with flexible allocation between control and storage, plus an articulatory loop (stored information decays quickly but is refreshed by rehearsal). Later additions: visuospatial sketchpad, episodic buffer. Critics called the executive a homunculus label.
quote: a limited capacity 'central executive' responsible for attention-demanding control processes
limits: Early dual-task studies gave little support for the proposed processing-versus-storage trade-off inside the executive. A better account came from Norman and Shallice's supervisory attentional system (competing schemata; control engaged only when automatic selection fails).
agent_relevance: Matches guardrail G1: control effort is spent only when automatic selection fails (a signal), not on a schedule.

source: Hitch, Allen and Baddeley (2024) The multicomponent model of working memory fifty years on (QJEP 78:222-239)
finding: Time-based decay in the phonological loop is now contested. Word-length effects are disputed (Caplan and Waters 1994; Lovatt et al. 2000) and Oberauer and Lewandowsky (2008) cast doubt on trace decay. The authors say the issue stays unresolved but the loop stays useful as a limited-capacity, speech-based store refreshed by rehearsal.
limits: Authors defend their own model; an independent view is in Oberauer's interference accounts. Computational loop models (Burgess and Hitch 1992; Page and Norris 1998) reproduce similarity, word-length and suppression effects but contain no executive control.
agent_relevance: Forgetting by interference, not by time, is the safer assumption. An LLM has no decay at all, so interference is the only forgetting mechanism that can apply.

source: Cowan (2001) The magical number 4 in short-term memory: A reconsideration of mental storage capacity (BBS 24:87-114, with peer commentary)
finding: Cowan argued that when chunking and rehearsal are blocked, pure short-term capacity is about 4 chunks (range 3-5), not 7. He proposed that the limit belongs to the focus of attention, which holds chunks inside a larger set of activated long-term memory.
numbers: Stated limit: a single central capacity limit averaging about four chunks. Four conditions to see it: (1) information overload limits chunks to single items, (2) steps block recoding, (3) performance discontinuities, (4) indirect effects.
quote: A single, central capacity limit averaging about four chunks is implicated along with other, noncapacity-limited sources.
limits: Target article followed by many commentaries, several challenging the number. A pure estimate holds only when inter-item associations cannot help recall; otherwise estimates are 'compound' and larger.
agent_relevance: Design rule: keep the live reasoning state to roughly 3-5 separate units. Beyond that, expect errors and externalize the rest.

source: Cowan (2001) The magical number 4 in short-term memory: A reconsideration of mental storage capacity (BBS 24:87-114, with peer commentary)
finding: Cowan et al. (1999): digits were presented in an ignored spoken stream while subjects played a rhyming-picture game; recall was a surprise test given 16 times. Items recalled stayed flat across list lengths, like Sperling's whole-report limit.
numbers: Ignored speech: adults 3.51 (SD 0.94, N=35), fourth graders 2.99 (N=26), first graders 2.34 (N=24). Attended: 5.43, 4.31, 3.48. Ratio attended/unattended 1.4-1.6 in all groups. Individual adult capacities ranged from about 2 to almost 6.
limits: Strict serial-position scoring. The wide individual range means 4 is a mean, not a constant. Attention at reception could add chunk-forming processes (the 1.4-1.6 ratio).
agent_relevance: A flat curve across list length is the signature of a true capacity limit. We can test an LLM the same way: accuracy should plateau, not rise, as items grow.

source: Cowan (2001) The magical number 4 in short-term memory: A reconsideration of mental storage capacity (BBS 24:87-114, with peer commentary)
finding: Luck and Vogel (1997) change detection, with limited output interference, gave the same limit of about 4. The limit applies to integrated objects, not to features.
numbers: Arrays of 1-12 colored squares, 100 ms display, 900 ms blank, same/different report: near perfect at 1-3 items, slightly worse at 4, much worse above. Objects with 4 feature dimensions were retained as well as objects with 1 feature.
limits: Described in Cowan's review (the Luck and Vogel paper itself was not opened). Later work on precision challenged the all-or-none object view (see slot versus resource line).
agent_relevance: Bind related facts into one object (one record with several fields) so they cost one slot, not several.

source: Cowan (2001) The magical number 4 in short-term memory: A reconsideration of mental storage capacity (BBS 24:87-114, with peer commentary)
finding: Subitizing and whole-report data show a sharp discontinuity near 4: errors near zero for 1-4 items, then a steep rise.
numbers: Mandler and Shebo (1982): near-zero errors for 1-4 items (1-3 at 200 ms), then about +15% errors per extra item up to near 100% error at 11 items. Henderson (1972): letters reported rose from about 3 (100 ms mask) to about 5.5 (1250 ms), showing fast transfer into the limited store. Sperling's highly trained subjects: capacity about 3.5-4.5.
limits: Few trained subjects in Sperling; subitizing could be a perceptual rather than a memory mechanism, as some commentators argued.
agent_relevance: Fits an agent rule: stepwise tasks whose live variables stay at 4 or fewer should be reliable, and error should jump after that.

source: Cowan (2001) The magical number 4 in short-term memory: A reconsideration of mental storage capacity (BBS 24:87-114, with peer commentary)
finding: Free-recall recency estimates, once rehearsal and long-term contributions are removed, give about 3 items. Delayed recency effects of 3-5 items still appear after distractor tasks, which challenges a pure short-term store.
numbers: Watkins (1974) estimates 2.21-3.43; by the Tulving-Colotla method 2.93-3.35. Bjork and Whitten (1974): recency of 3-5 items after up to 42 s of arithmetic between pairs.
limits: Delayed recency is a known problem for any pure short-term store account (Glenberg and Swanson 1986 offered a ratio-rule account).
agent_relevance: Recency is cheap but not proof of a capacity-limited store; for LLMs, recency bias is a strong separate effect to control.

source: Commentary on Cowan (2001) citing Wickelgren et al. (1980) and McElree and Dosher (1989, 1993), in BBS 24
finding: A peer commentary using speed-accuracy-tradeoff data argued that true focal attention holds only one item, not 3-4. Retrieval is 50% faster only for the last-studied item.
numbers: Wickelgren et al. (1980): 16-item probe recognition; retrieval speed constant across all positions except the last; 50% faster with no intervening items. Replicated with Sternberg and recognition procedures.
quote: we are only able to maintain one temporally extended event or epoch in focal attention
limits: A competing view (one-item focus inside a larger activated region), so 4 is the activated set and 1 is the focus. Numbers come from the commentary text, not the original SAT papers.
agent_relevance: Two-level design: one item being worked on, a small set of about 3-4 immediately available items, and the rest externalized.

source: Souza et al. (2014) description of Bays and Husain (2008), Wilken and Ma (2004), Luck and Vogel (1997), Zhang and Luck (2008)
finding: Two families explain the capacity limit in visual working memory. Flexible-resource: a continuous resource is divided across objects, so more objects means lower precision for each. Discrete-capacity: a few slots; an object gets a slot with good precision or nothing (slot+averaging lets several slots go to one object).
limits: Taken from a 2014 paper, not the original Zhang and Luck or Bays and Husain papers (PMC blocked). The debate is not settled; both models fit once extended.
agent_relevance: Unsettled whether to treat the limit as 'N items' or 'shared precision'. For an LLM, shared precision (more items lowers accuracy for each) matches the PI-LLM and n-back curves better.

source: Souza, Rerko, Lin and Oberauer (2014) Focused attention improves working memory: implications for flexible-resource and discrete-capacity models (Atten Percept Psychophys 76:2080-2102)
finding: Focusing attention on one held object (delay condition: cue shown, report delayed) improved recall by reducing guessing and transposition errors, not by raising precision. Both a flexible-resource and a discrete-capacity model fit only when extended with graded spatial transposition errors.
numbers: Experiment 1: 16 students, 6 colored disks. Experiment 2: 22 students (21 analysed), set sizes 1-8, 1000 ms retention, cue then delayed versus immediate report. Benefit from focusing = fewer guesses and transpositions.
limits: Small samples, colour-wheel recall only. Authors say a higher share of capacity given to the target explains the benefit.
agent_relevance: Supports a scaffold step that re-reads the one needed item before answering: refocusing reduces retrieval failures even when stored content is unchanged.

source: Gong, Wan and Wang (2024) Working Memory Capacity of ChatGPT: An Empirical Study (AAAI 2024; arXiv 2305.03731)
finding: ChatGPT (gpt-3.5-turbo) shows a human-like fall in n-back detection sensitivity d' as n goes from 1 to 3. Capacity is defined as the n where d' drops to about 1. Four verbal variants: base, with noise symbols, with feedback, with chain-of-thought reasoning.
numbers: 50 blocks per n in 1-3, 24 trials each (8 match, 16 nonmatch), temperature 1. Apart from the noise variant, d' falls to about 1 at n=3 (capacity about 3). Noise lowers capacity significantly.
quote: ChatGPT has a working memory capacity limit strikingly similar to that of humans.
limits: Only n up to 3 tested; human capacity at n=3 is itself a rough convention. Feedback and chain-of-thought did not remove the drop. GPT-4 tested only to n=3 for cost.
agent_relevance: N-back shows a 3-ish interference-limited capacity in chat LLMs although the stream fits easily in context. Use n-back as a cheap capacity probe for any model the agent uses.

source: Gong, Wan and Wang (2024) Working Memory Capacity of ChatGPT: An Empirical Study (AAAI 2024; arXiv 2305.03731)
finding: Spatial n-back (grid positions) also declined with n. Larger grids gave higher d', which the authors read as less interference between items. Spatial variants requiring row/column reasoning were harder.
numbers: Grids 3x3, 4x4, 5x5, 7x7 tested; capacity higher with larger grid. Variants: noise, feedback, chain-of-thought, two abstract rules (same row/column, or row-or-column-not-both).
limits: Grid-size explanation is the authors' guess; no human data for comparison. Single model for spatial variants.
agent_relevance: Distinct, dissimilar items interfere less; give each tracked variable a distinct label format.

source: Gong, Wan and Wang (2024) Working Memory Capacity of ChatGPT: An Empirical Study (AAAI 2024; arXiv 2305.03731)
finding: Model comparison on verbal n-back: GPT-4 clearly above GPT-3.5, and both far above small open models. Small open models were nearly indistinguishable at a very low level.
numbers: Models: Bloomz-7B, Bloomz-7B1-mt, ChatGLM-6B v1.0 and v1.1, GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Vicuna-7B, Vicuna-13B. Kruskal-Wallis across n for GPT-4: H=58.5, p=3.95e-12, effect size 0.65.
limits: The appendix tables are garbled in the PDF text; only the GPT-4 row was read with confidence. No effect of n for several small models (floor).
agent_relevance: Pick the model for the agent's slot-filling steps by a capacity probe, not by parameter count alone.

source: Gong and Zhang (2024) Self-Attention Limits Working Memory Capacity of Transformer-Based Models (NeurIPS 2024 workshop; arXiv 2409.10715)
finding: Small decoder-only transformers trained on n-back learn to attend to position i-N. Accuracy falls as N rises, and the entropy of the attention matrix rises, so spread-out attention is proposed as a cause of the limit.
numbers: Alphabet of 20 consonants; sequences of 24 letters, 8 matches and 16 nonmatches; N in 1-6; 800 training and 200 test sequences per N. 1-layer 1-head: Kruskal-Wallis H=38.5, p<.001, effect 0.248; log decline up to N=6. Larger models reached over 95% at all N but still declined slightly.
limits: Correlational (entropy versus accuracy), toy models trained from scratch, a workshop paper. Not shown for pretrained LLMs.
agent_relevance: Capacity loss comes from attention spread, so short, clean prompts that put the needed item near the point of use should help (untested here).

source: Xiong, Ji-An, Huang, Wilson, Lee and Wei (2026) In-context superposition: human-like working memory interference in large language models (COLM 2026; arXiv 2604.09670)
finding: LLM working memory limits look like interference limits. A two-layer transformer solves n-back perfectly (100% accuracy), but ten pretrained LLMs decline with load and show recency bias, lure effects and stimulus-set-size effects like humans. Several memories are stored in entangled form ('in-context superposition').
numbers: Pearson r between interference condition and accuracy across models: lures -.51 / -.32 (two evaluation modes), smaller stimulus set -.30 / -.26, transition statistics .36 / -.62. Target alignment correlates .78 / .76 with recall; letter decodability -.42 / -.14.
quote: working memory capacity reflects the ability to select task-relevant information under interference
limits: Ten open-weight models, non-thinking mode; r values pooled over models and N, so not independent. Lures: with probability 0.25 the input was replaced by the item at N-1 or N+1.
agent_relevance: Interference, not storage, is the limit. Design rule: remove near-duplicate items (stale values, similar names) from the working prompt.

source: Xiong, Ji-An, Huang, Wilson, Lee and Wei (2026) In-context superposition: human-like working memory interference in large language models (COLM 2026; arXiv 2604.09670)
finding: A causal edit that suppresses letter-identity directions in the residual stream raised n-back accuracy, most in weaker models. Mean n-back accuracy tracks broader model ability across ten models.
numbers: n-back accuracy (mean of N=1-4) correlated with MMLU-Pro .78/.70, GPQA Diamond .88/.72, IFEval .69/.82 (autoregressive / teacher-forced); log parameter count did not significantly predict any of the three. Human reference: r = .31-.78 with reasoning.
limits: Best intervention settings were chosen and tested on the same trials, so held-out gain is untested. Only ten models; correlational.
agent_relevance: A model with a better n-back score is likely better at tracking state; a cheap proxy for model choice.

source: Wang and Sun (2025) Unable to Forget: Proactive Interference Reveals Working Memory Limits in LLMs Beyond Context Length (ICML 2025 workshop; arXiv 2506.08184)
finding: Proactive interference test (PI-LLM): a stream of key-value updates, only the last value per key is asked. Retrieval accuracy falls log-linearly toward zero as earlier (outdated) values per key accumulate, even though the answer is easy to find. Errors are overwritten values.
numbers: 46 keys fixed, updates per key 3 to 400 (log spaced); 30 models, 0.6B to 637B parameters. Regression: parameter size class predicts interference endurance score (t=3.03, p=0.005, N=30; R2=0.261); Spearman rho between size and IES 0.673 (p=0.0016); context window length had no significant effect.
limits: Workshop paper, synthetic task, one group; no independent replication found. Natural-language 'forget the old values' instructions gave only marginal gains.
agent_relevance: Stale values in the prompt hurt more than length. The scaffold should delete or overwrite superseded state in code, not tell the model to ignore it.

source: Wang and Sun (2025) Unable to Forget: Proactive Interference Reveals Working Memory Limits in LLMs Beyond Context Length (ICML 2025 workshop; arXiv 2506.08184)
finding: The failure looks like a hard limit, not smooth noise: step-like drops in sequential-update tests, and wrong answers are mostly earlier values, many anchored to the earliest value. The authors report humans do these tasks with high accuracy.
numbers: A fixed-length control (input length constant, interference load rising) still lowers accuracy log-linearly.
limits: Human comparison is cited from the literature, not run by these authors in the parts read.
agent_relevance: Keep one current value per variable in the working state.

source: Huang, Sun, Wang and Dredze (2026) On the Failure of Latent State Persistence in Large Language Models (arXiv 2505.10571 v5)
finding: LLMs cannot hold a hidden variable across turns without writing it into context. Three tests: number guessing (probability mass over a full state space should sum to 1), yes-no game (consistency over many questions), hidden-variable tracking (apply moves to a number set aside).
numbers: Yes-no game, 60 objects, up to 250 queries: GPT-4o-mini passes 0% of trials (mean steps to contradiction 41.4), GPT-4o 13.5% (mean 74.6). Hidden-variable test: 17 models, 150 trials each, most near-zero success; chain-of-thought lifted base models to 10-30%; long-reasoning models (o-series, DeepSeek-R1) near perfect or much higher. About 67-69% of correct o1-mini and o4-mini answers were the number 7.
limits: The 'no latent state' reading is the authors' interpretation; success after chain-of-thought is consistent with state becoming visible tokens.
agent_relevance: Strong support for the schema rule that state lives in explicit, code-held text, not 'in the model's head'.

source: Aichberger and Hochreiter (2026) Unlocking the Working Memory of Large Language Models for Latent Reasoning (arXiv 2605.30343)
finding: Reasoning in Memory (RiM): fixed blocks of special tokens act as a latent workspace so the model reasons without writing step tokens; two-stage curriculum (ground with step supervision, then anytime answer refinement).
numbers: GSM8K: 2.5-7.5 points above the strongest Coconut variant and 12.6-18.2 points above direct-answer fine-tuning; GSM-Hard: 0.7-1.8 above Coconut and 3.5-5.2 above direct answer; models GPT-2, Llama-3.2-1B, Llama-3.2-3B; 16-split cross-validation for checkpoint choice.
limits: Needs fine-tuning, small models, math word problems only. The 'working memory' label is a metaphor, not a test of human WM effects. Table rows were garbled in extraction, so only the paragraph gains are used.
agent_relevance: Training can add latent working space, but our agent does not train. Its route is explicit external state.

source: Baddeley (2000) episodic buffer, via Wikipedia page on Baddeley's model of working memory
finding: The episodic buffer was added in 2000 as a limited-capacity system that links information across domains into episodes. Motivation: amnesic patients recalled stories at a level the phonological loop could not hold. The page gives no numbers.
limits: Secondary source (Wikipedia). A claim on the page about a 2026 renaming is unverified and not used. Loop evidence listed there: phonological similarity, articulatory suppression.
agent_relevance: A multi-field record bound together is a natural unit (the buffer idea); supports storing a compact 'episode' object.

source: Daneman and Carpenter (1980) Individual differences in working memory and reading
finding: Reading span (hold final words while reading sentences) predicted reading comprehension better than simple digit span. Background knowledge; not opened this session.
limits: Specific correlations not opened; fill in on a later pass.
agent_relevance: Processing plus storage in the same task is the right test for a thinking agent, not plain recall.

source: Engle, Kane and Tuholski (1999) and Engle (2002) Working memory capacity as executive attention
finding: Executive-attention view: individual differences in working-memory capacity reflect control of attention (keeping goals active and blocking interference), not storage size. Cited by Gong et al. 2024 and Xiong et al. 2026 as the framing. Not opened.
limits: No numbers recorded.
agent_relevance: Same as G1: a control layer that keeps the goal and blocks distractors.

source: Barrouillet, Bernardin and Camos (2004) time-based resource sharing; Oberauer (2002) embedded-processes and interference accounts
finding: Competing accounts for processing-plus-storage tasks: time-based resource sharing (attention alternates between processing and refreshing memory traces; more busy time means more forgetting), and interference accounts (Oberauer) with a focus of attention of one item inside a region of direct access. Background knowledge; not opened.
limits: No numbers recorded; to read in angle B.
agent_relevance: A long, busy reasoning step leaves less time to refresh earlier items; in an LLM the analogue is load per step.
